accuracy.evidence: Matches DfE Development Matters 3 and 4 year olds, Understanding the World ('Talk about the differences between materials and changes they notice'; 'Use all their senses in hands-on exploration of natural materials') and the EYFS ELG The Natural World. Timescales were checked as typical, not exact: a small ice cube melts in roughly an hour at room temperature or in sun, a shallow puddle dries within a day on a warm day, and a banana browns over several days as starch and pigment break down; cut apple browns through enzymic oxidation.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented early-science errors: melted ice has 'gone away' rather than turned to water (Driver et al. on change of state), a changed object is a 'new' object (identity through change), only big changes count while small details and unchanged things are ignored, and ordering a sequence backwards. Each is a prediction option, a lab feedback message or a challenge distractor.

lab_distinct.evidence: Five mechanics specific to observation over time: a time slider that melts an ice cube while the water level rises, a Before/Now spot-the-change with two unchanged decoys, a draggable magnifier that clips and zooms the scene 3.2 times to reveal details too small to see, a four-stop clock line comparing fast and slow changes side by side, and a first-then-now ordering of change pictures. None of these appear in other flagship labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child makes the change happen and sees the ice become water (not vanish), then compares two states and must also notice what did not change, then learns that looking up close finds what a quick look misses, then discovers rates differ (ice in an hour, banana over a week), and finally sequences the change in words. The confirm text names each idea only after the action.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'The cup sits in a warm room. What will the ice do? Stay the same' (the slider melts it), and 'Which changes first? The banana' (the 1 hour stop shows the ice melted and the banana unchanged).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve distinct m= wrong-answer messages: ice did not go away, nobody ate it, the puddle got smaller not bigger, something did change, same banana not a new one, yellow to brown is a change, a far look misses tiny things, eyes must be open, ice is fast and bananas slow, the two rates differ, browning does not reverse, and the slice does not grow.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short read-aloud sentences with concrete words (ice, cup, banana, bug, seed) and the frames before and now, first, then and now. Adult text stays within the family limit while naming observation, compare, hand lens and change over time. Canvas prompts are under eight words and the young class keeps tap targets large.

no_filler.evidence: Passes the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate. Each kid paragraph does one job (melting, a slow change, looking up close, fast, slow or no change); each adult paragraph has one purpose (curriculum aim, vocabulary and timescales, mistakes, what the lab does); the family tip is a concrete two-plate experiment.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passes on iPhone 13 (390 px). Phone screenshots of every step were checked: the slider and clock stops span the width with labels above, the Before/Now rows stack vertically so all five objects fit, the magnifier stays inside the canvas, and every action also has a full-width button row.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (Earlier or Later, one button per object, magnifier spots Top, Middle, Bottom and Left, one button per time, Picture 1 to 3 then Put it next). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with what changed, what was found and the current time. axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes.
